title: Performance considerations
learningObjectives: Explain performance considerations and apply the concept in maintainable CSS.

understand.concept: Animation performance depends on the properties being animated, the number and size of affected elements, and browser rendering work. Transform and opacity are often more efficient candidates than properties that trigger layout, but actual performance should be measured.
understand.whyItMatters: Excessive animation can drain battery, cause dropped frames, and distract users. Profile on representative devices, keep animations purposeful, and avoid unnecessary will-change declarations.
understand.analogy: A smooth animation is like a light object moving without repeatedly rebuilding the whole scene.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy simplifies the idea; actual cascade, inheritance, and rendering follow CSS specifications.

explain.narrative: This simple effect changes transform and opacity. Measure performance rather than assuming every animation is cheap.

examples.explanation: This simple effect changes transform and opacity. Measure performance rather than assuming every animation is cheap.
examples.expectedOutput: A rendered example showing the relevant CSS behaviour.

practise.guidedTask: Compare animating transform with animating width on a group of cards. Use performance tools and record any difference on a representative device.
practise.independentTask: Build a small component or page section that uses the concept. Test alternate content and, where relevant, right-to-left direction or reduced-motion settings.

questions.prompt: What is a maintainable way to use CSS features across a project?
options: Use clear reusable rules and test computed behaviour
Copy unrelated declarations into every component
Ignore writing direction and user preferences
questions.answer: Use clear reusable rules and test computed behaviour
questions.explanation: Reusable CSS should remain understandable and work across relevant content and user settings.
